items.title: Avakian George — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I met a classmate named Jerry King, who became my closest friend

ctx.x: Were the other bands – was it easier for the other bands to be heard because they were white?

Oh yes, definitely. I remember that Ellington was very seldom heard on the radio. All of these black musicians were not heard much. I got into Ellington because of the popular songs that he wrote and recorded. I remember one of the first ones that I ever bought was Sophisticated Lady, on Brunswick. The path led, of course, into other Ellington music. By the time I graduated from Horace Mann, I had quite a few Ellington Brunswicks. items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: mainly with a classmate named Jerry King, who was also an enthusiastic young collector... there are two years worth of labels made out by King and Avakian.

ctx.x: You had mentioned Marshall Stearns as a very important person in your life.

Absolutely. Marshall Stearns was a graduate school student. We all thought he was a college professor because he had a byline that gave 20 Lake Place, New Haven, Connecticut as the place to write to him about questions about jazz and so forth. But to my surprise when I enrolled as a freshman in 1937 I found that he was living just off campus with his wife and going to the graduate school to get a Ph.D. in English Literature.
